panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E punch biopsy from left arm of mixed-infiltrate type A LyP showing dermal/subcutis mixed lymphoid infiltrate, matching wedge-shaped dermal infiltrate vocabulary term. B: CD30 IHC shows CD30-positive large Hodgkin-like cells interspersed in LyP infiltrate, direct match to CD30-positive atypical cells finding. C: CD3 IHC highlights the dense reactive T-cell component of the type A LyP wedge-shaped mixed dermal infiltrate; CD3 specificity captured as proposed finding. D: BCL2 IHC shows same LyP lymphoid meshwork and Hodgkin-like cells with strong BCL2 staining; underlying infiltrate qualifies as wedge-shaped infiltrate, BCL2 captured as proposed since not in vocabulary.

panels.figure_caption: Immunohistochemical analysis of mixed-infiltrate type A lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP). The punch biopsy from the left arm identified a diffuse infiltration of small lymphocytes and few large-sized Hodgkin-like cells that were prevalent in the dermis and subcutis, while largely sparing the epidermis (A, original magnification, ×10). in_text_mentions: A 51‐year‐old Indian man presented with a 2‐month history of foot ulcers causing pain on exertion. Examination revealed two shallow, oval ulcers on the right dorsal foot with central eschars (Figure 1a). Inspection of the surrounding skin showed atrophic scarring, suggesting previously healed lesions. The patient had no systemic symptoms and no palpable lymphadenopathy. A diagnosis of vasculitis was considered.

The patient presented 3 months later with four new ulcerated and crusted plaques on the right anterior shin (Figure 1b). The previously identified lesions on the right foot had resolved. A skin biopsy of one of the new lesions was performed.

Histology revealed widespread epidermal and dermal necrosis with central ulceration. In the dermis, histiocytes, eosinophils, and infiltrates of atypical lymphocytes were found in an angiocentric pattern (Figure 1c). Lymphocytes invading the vessel walls had led to angiodestruction. Immunohistochemical investigations showed that CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5 and CD7 were positive. Additionally, CD30 and CD8 were focally positive (Figure 1d).

in_text_mentions: Cutaneous lesions involved the limbs in all patients (Figure 1A). Additional sites included the trunk (5/9, 56%), hands (4/9, 44%), gluteal region (2/9, 22%), and face (2/9, 22%). Two patients showed diffuse involvement, while no mucosal lesions were documented. Lesions ranged from 2 to 3 mm papules to papulonodular lesions up to 1 cm in diameter. Ulceration, crusting, or necrotic evolution occurred in 6/9 patients (67%), including both children younger than 5 years. Residual scarring and/or pigmentary changes were observed in two patients (Cases 1 and 9), first documented 7 and 9 months after

findings were heterogeneous (Table 2). Type A was the most frequent subtype (5/9, 56%), followed by single cases of type B, type D, and type E (Figure 2); one patient showed overlapping type A/C features (Figures 1B–E). CD30 expression was detected in all cases, although one showed only partial and variable expression. T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement analysis was available in five patients and showed monoclonal TCRγ rearrangement or a dominant monoclonal pattern in 4/5 (80%), including one case with combined TCRβ and TCRγ clonality. Serial biopsies were obtained in 5/9 patients (56%).
